tells: 1. Laugh gestures read as distress, not amusement: pink-jacket man covers one eye like he's wiping tears or facepalming, and the blonde holds her temple as if she has a headache. There's no torso pump or shoulder shake to sell the laugh (club-2-mid.png, far left and centre-right front tables)

2. The laugh is carried only by the two or three hero tables. The red-jacket man and the purple-top woman barely change from t=12.0 to 13.0, and the back rows stay static, so the room doesn't swell (club-5-strip.png, left edge and centre-right; back rows across the top)

3. The face close is a mouth-only expression: the lips part but the cheeks don't rise and the eyes don't narrow. The chin-rest hand has stiff, evenly curled fingers that look posed, and the blurred blonde behind has a smeared, stretched neck and jaw (club-4-face.png, centre face and hand; left background)

4. In the wide, the front tables sit in near-identical rest poses (forearms on the table, hands clasped by the candle, upright spines, everyone squared to the camera), which reads like a seating chart, not a room listening (club-1-wide.png, front row across the centre)

5. Stray elements break the illusion: a lone woman on a stool at an empty table, a floating red glow dot, a hard diagonal line at the right edge, and a dark silhouette standing flat against the bright bar (club-6-held.png, right third; club-1-wide.png, bar at centre-right)

1. In the wide, the front row sits in a symmetrical class-photo pose: knees apart, hands on knees or clasped in the lap, spines vertical, heads square to the lens. The held frame is almost identical, so the stalls look frozen (theatre-1-wide.png and theatre-6-held.png, the two lit front rows)

2. The back of the house is cut-out silhouettes: flat dark figures that look like they're standing at uniform head height, with no seat backs and no movement, like a cardboard crowd (theatre-2-mid.png and theatre-3-mid.png, top half; theatre-1-wide.png, upper rows)

3. The laugh timing is a step, not a build. Nothing changes from t=12.0 to 12.4, then three or four mouths open together at 12.6 with no lean or head toss, and the back rows never react (theatre-5-strip.png, all six frames, front row centre)

4. Row depth and scale look wrong: second-row heads float high above the front row's shoulders, as if they're perched on seat backs, and the far-left man on row two is lit like a cut-out against the black (theatre-1-wide.png, centre rows; theatre-2-mid.png, upper left)

5. The face close has an open-mouth laugh with dead eyes (no cheek lift, no crinkle), a chunky low-poly hair helmet, and fingers bent in a stiff claw at the jaw (theatre-4-face.png, centre face, hairline and hand)

1. Hair rendering breaks at TV distance: the yellow-shirt man's hair edge is dithered and stippled, the afro has a visible seam and hair cards sticking up, and the cap brim and head merge (openmic-4-face.png, top right of the head; openmic-6-held.png, centre afro and right yellow-shirt head)

2. The wide is packed so tightly that bodies interpenetrate: shoulders overlap neighbours, the black-hoodie woman seems wedged between rows, and the front row leans forward with hands on knees in near-identical poses (openmic-1-wide.png, front two rows centre)
3. The teeth and mouths in the laugh look like dark braces or gritted teeth, so the green-top and red-haired women read as grimacing, not laughing (openmic-2-mid.png, centre-right faces)

4. Some necks bend unnaturally: the cap man in the held frame juts forward and down off his shoulders, and the yellow-shirt man's head sits stiff on a rigid torso while the people next to him move (openmic-6-held.png, far left; openmic-3-mid.png, centre)

5. The face close shows a neutral half-smile with eyes not quite converging on the stage, and the hair-to-skin boundary is cut sharply against a soft background. It reads as a game cutscene, not a reaction (openmic-4-face.png, centre face)
